rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān derives al-Ṣafāʾ’s alif from wāw, supported by ṣafw and ṣafwān.
rows.anchor: ألفه منقلبة عن واو لقولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis treats ṣafā as a collective noun whose singular is ṣafāh; another treats it as singular with plurals ṣafiyy and aṣfāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو اسم جنس بينه وبين مفرده تاء التأنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural fuʿūl may have either a damma or kasra, like ʿuṣiyy; ṣafā is smooth stone, stone unmixed with soil, or a large rock.
rows.anchor: وتضم الصاد في فعول وتكسر، كعصي، وهو الحجر الأملس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marwah is singular of marw, a collective for stones variously described as soft, hard, small and sharp-edged, black, white, or hard and white.
rows.anchor: وهي الحجارة الصغار التي فيها لين. وقيل: الحجارة الصلبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unidentified poetic line uses marw in describing stones left behind when someone departs.
rows.anchor: فترى المرو إذا ما هجرت ... عن يديها كالفراش المشفتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah are established names of two known mountains; the definite article is fixed through exclusive usage, like al-Bayt for the Kaʿbah and al-Najm for the Pleiades.
rows.anchor: والصفا والمروة في الآية: علمان لجبلين معروفين، والألف واللام لزمتا فيهما للغلبة

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari defines the ritual signs as markers God recommended and commanded people to uphold, as heard by al-Harawi.
rows.anchor: قال الهروي: سمعت الأزهري يقول: هي العلائم التي ندب الله إليها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj includes every standing place, ritual site, saʿy place, and sacrificial site within the ritual signs.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: كل ما كان من موقف ومشهد ومسعى ومذبح.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root shaʿara means to perceive or know; Arabs also call a house a sign, and sacrificial marking derives from the same root.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدمت لنا هذه المادة، أعني مادة شعر، أي أدرك وعلم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥajj originally means repeated intention; ʿumrah means visiting, or, according to another view, intending; they became names for the two known pilgrimages to the House.
rows.anchor: الحج: القصد مرة بعد أخرى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Janāḥ first denotes inclining toward sin and then denotes sin itself; taṭawwaʿ is derived from obedience and submission.
rows.anchor: الجناح: الميل إلى المأثم، ثم أطلق على الإثم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some treat layl as a collective like tamr, Abū Ḥayyān says it is singular and has no attested plural; layālī is plural of laylah.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه مفرد، ولا يحفظ جمعا لليل، وأخطأ من ظن

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Fāris says layl is also the name of a bird, reportedly the young of the bustard.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن فارس: بعض الطير يسمى ليلا، ويقال: إنه ولد الحبارى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nahār has regular plurals nahr and anhura; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the claim that it is an unpluralizable verbal noun.
rows.anchor: فجمعه نهر وأنهرة، كقذل وأقذلة، وهما جمعان مقيسان فيه.

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet told ʿAdī that the fast’s white thread is the brightness of day and its black thread the darkness of night.
rows.anchor: قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم لعدي: «إنما هو بياض النهار وسواد الليل»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent linguistic boundary of daytime begins with dawn and ends at sunset.
rows.anchor: وظاهر اللغة أنه من وقت الإسفار. وقال النضر

rows.speaker: النضر بن شميل
rows.claim: Al-Naḍr says daytime begins at sunrise, excluding the preceding period.
rows.anchor: وقال النضر بن شميل: ويغلب أول النهار طلوع الشمس.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj places the start of daytime at the sun’s first appearance, adducing Umayyah’s verse about sunrise before dawn’s final night.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج، في (كتاب الأنواء) : أول النهار ذرور الشمس

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī says daytime runs from sunrise to sunset, while dawn until sunrise belongs jointly to night and day.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: من طلوع الشمس إلى غروبها نهار، ومن الفجر إلى طلوعها مشترك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fulk is a shared form for singular and plural with the same vowel pattern; singular can be dualized as fulkān and is masculine, while feminine agreement can reflect plural use.
rows.anchor: والذي نذهب إليه أنه لفظ مشترك بين المفرد والجمع، وأن حركاته في الجمع حركاته في المفرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baṯṯ means to spread, disperse, and make manifest; poetry depicts a snake and scorpion spread through the land.
rows.anchor: بث: نشر وفرق وأظهر. قال الشاعر:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dābbah covers every animal; ʿAlqamah’s image of birds’ movement answers those who exclude birds. Its feminine ending may be literal or intensive, and it applies to either sex.
rows.anchor: ورد قول من أخرج منه الطير بقول علقمة: كأنهم صابت عليهم سحابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taṣrīf is the verbal noun of ṣarafa, whose sense is turning or sending something back.
rows.anchor: التصريف: مصدر صرف، ومعناه: راجع للصرف، وهو الرد.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah calls ʿUmārah’s use of ariyāḥ in poetry ungrammatical.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وقد لحن في هذه اللفظة عمارة بن عقيل بن بلال بن جرير،

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abū Ḥātim also says ariyāḥ is impermissible, though ʿUmārah challenged him with the familiar form riyāḥ.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حاتم: إن الأرياح لا يجوز، فقال له عمارة: ألا تسمع قولهم: رياح؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān recalls attested classical poetry using ariyāḥ, formed from the singular despite the sound-change cause disappearing in the plural, as in ʿīd/aʿyād.
rows.anchor: وفي محفوظي قديما أن الأرياح جاءت في شعر بعض فصحاء العرب

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī derives saḥāb from withdrawal and also reports ḥabā, crawling, as another name for clouds.
rows.anchor: السحاب: اسم جنس، المفرد سحابة، سمي بذلك لأنه ينسحب، كما يقال له: حبى، لأنه يحبو، قاله أبو علي.

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines taskhīr as coercing something into action, stronger than mere compulsion; Abū Ḥayyān first glosses it as subjection and making something compliant.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب: التسخير: القهر على الفعل، وهو أبلغ من الإكراه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal noun ḥubb follows the pattern ḥabba yaḥubbu; aḥabba is more common than ḥabba, and maḥbūb and muḥibb are more common than their alternatives.
rows.anchor: الحب: مصدر حب يحب، وقياس مضارعه يحب بالضم، لأنه من المضاعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most reciters read an yaṭṭawwafa; Anas, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Sīrīn, and Shahr read an lā, as do the codices of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allāh.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور: أن يطوف. وقرأ أنس وابن عباس وابن سيرين وشهر: أن لا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading treats lā as extra, equating both recitations; Abū Ḥayyān says that is unnecessary because exemption from blame for acting also permits leaving it, and the reading with lā explicitly exempts leaving.
rows.anchor: وخرج ذلك على زيادة لا، نحو: ما منعك ألا تسجد ؟

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is among those who hold saʿy between the two hills is optional and that deliberate or inadvertent omission incurs no penalty, though one should not omit it.
rows.anchor: وهو مروي عن ابن عباس، وأنس، وابن الزبير، وعطاء، ومجاهد، وأحمد بن حنبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says positions making saʿy a pillar, a duty compensated by sacrifice, or subject to penalties by number of circuits require a clear text abrogating this Qurʾānic wording.
rows.anchor: يحتاج إلى نص جلي ينسخ هذا النص القرآني

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾishah told ʿUrwah that the wording does not entail that saʿy is obligatory; it merely removes blame for performing it and thus leaves the person free to do or omit it.
rows.anchor: وقول عائشة لعروة حين قال لها: أرأيت قول الله: فلا جناح عليه أن يطوف بهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording requires saʿy at the two hills themselves, but specifies neither its manner nor its number of circuits.
rows.anchor: وظاهر هذا الطواف أن يكون بالصفا والمروة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Regional scholars agree that jogging during saʿy is a Sunnah.
rows.anchor: واتفق علماء الأمصار على أن الرمل في السعي سنة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Via ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās says one may rush through Makkah’s valley or not; he means the brisk pace in the valley bottom.
rows.anchor: وروى عطاء، عن ابن عباس: من شاء سعى بمسيل مكة، ومن شاء لم يسع

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar said he walked because he saw the Prophet walk, and ran because he saw him run; the Prophet ran to show the polytheists his strength.
rows.anchor: وكان عمر يمشي بين الصفا والمروة وقال: إن مشيت، فقد رأيت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يمشي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Prophet ran to show strength to polytheists, the ruling may have ended with its cause or may remain legislated after the cause disappeared.
rows.anchor: فيحتمل أن يزول الحكم بزوال سببه، ويحتمل مشروعيته دائما، وإن زال السبب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanafīs and their associates dislike riding during saʿy; Mālik forbids riding during saʿy or ṭawāf without excuse and requires a sacrifice, with further remedies depending on proximity to the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: والركوب في السعي بينهما مكروه عند أبي حنيفة وأصحابه، ولا يجوز عند مالك

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: When Umm Salamah complained, the Prophet told her to perform ṭawāf behind the people while mounted; the report does not say he ordered a sacrifice.
rows.anchor: وشكت أم سلمة إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال: «طوفي من وراء الناس وأنت راكبة» .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars distinguish riding on an animal, which suffices, from being carried on a person, which does not.
rows.anchor: وفرق بعض أهل العلم فقال: إن طاف على ظهر بعير أجزاه، أو على ظهر إنسان لم يجزه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dual pronoun bi-himā does not require beginning saʿy at al-Ṣafā, though all scholars prescribe beginning there.
rows.anchor: وكون الضمير مثنى في قوله: بهما، لا يدل على البداءة بالصفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mālik and the well-known Ḥanafī position cancel a lap begun at al-Marwah; another Ḥanafī report imposes nothing, comparing it to the sequence of ablution.
rows.anchor: فمذهب مالك، ومشهور مذهب أبي حنيفة، أنه يلغى ذلك الشوط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read yaṭṭawwafa as an assimilated form of yataṭawwaf; Abū Ḥamzah reads it from ṭāfa yaṭūfu, while Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū al-Sammāl read yuṭāfu, a passive form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يطوف وأصله يتطوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects two grammarians’ parses of an yaṭṭawwafa as a nominative predicate or accusative circumstantial clause as unsound.
rows.anchor: وهذان القولان ساقطان، ولولا تسطيرهما في بعض كتب التفسير لما ذكرتهما.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception is connected: repentance may mean leaving disbelief for Islam or leaving concealment for disclosure.
rows.anchor: إلا الذين تابوا: هذا استثناء متصل، ومعنى تابوا عن الكفر إلى الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repair may mean restoring hearts corrupted by disbelief, repairing one’s relationship with God, or guiding people previously led astray.
rows.anchor: وأصلحوا ما أفسدوا من قلوبهم بمخالطة الكفر لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may clarify the concealed truth, demonstrate repentance by destroying wine, disclose Muhammad’s description in earlier scriptures, confess deception, or publicize repentance as a model.
rows.anchor: وبينوا: أي الحق الذي كتموه، أو صدق توبتهم بكسر الخمر وإراقتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s turning toward the repentant removes the curse; the closing names al-Tawwāb and al-Raḥīm encourage repentance and signal that God will show mercy to those who return.
rows.anchor: أتوب عليهم: أي أعطف عليهم، ومن تاب الله عليه لا تلحقه لعنة.

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd warns against telling people what their understanding cannot bear, because it may become a trial for some of them.
rows.anchor: روي عن عبد الله أنه قال: ما أنت بمحدث قوما حديثا لا تبلغه عقولهم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet instructs speakers to address people in terms they understand; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وروي عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: «حدث الناس بما يفهمون» .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Concealing revealed religious knowledge is forbidden when the teacher is safe and has a duty to teach; other kinds of knowledge need not be disclosed.
rows.anchor: منها أن كتمان العلم حرام، يعنون علم الشريعة لقوله: ما أنزلنا من البينات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Explicit and inferred religious rulings alike should be taught when required; a teacher who fears for himself is excused, and one not personally appointed must teach when asked.
rows.anchor: والمنصوص عليه من الشرائع والمستنبط منه في الحكم سواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He lists prohibitions on charging for teaching, teaching Qurʾān to a non-Muslim before conversion, arming an adversary or ruler with harmful arguments, and teaching concessions known to enable sin.
rows.anchor: ومنها: تحريم الأجرة على تعليم العلم، وقد أجازه بعض العلماء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The obligation to clarify revealed guidance entails accepting a solitary report, since its content includes both explicit and inferred rulings.
rows.anchor: ومنها: وجوب قبول خبر الواحد، لأنه لا يجب عليه البيان إلا وقد وجب عليهم قبول قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars permit cursing unbelievers collectively but not a named unbeliever; some require it. Ibn al-ʿArabī permits cursing a particular unbeliever, while scholars report agreement against cursing sinful Muslims.
rows.anchor: وجمهور العلماء على جواز لعن الكفار جملة من غير تعيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Valid repentance must visibly reverse prior conduct: a former apostate returns to Islam and its practices, and a sinner returns to good works and leaves corrupt company; words alone or repentance from only one sin do not suffice.
rows.anchor: أن التوبة المعتبرة شرعا أن يظهر التائب خلاف ما كان عليه في الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For a nominative reading of angels and all people after God’s curse, Abū Ḥayyān prefers al-Farrāʾ’s restriction: a tanwinned verbal noun is not followed by a nominative agent.
rows.anchor: والفراء يقول: لا يجوز ذلك، بل إذا نون المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He offers three alternatives for the nominative reading: supply an implicit verb, coordinate to “God’s curse” with a deleted noun, or make angels and people a subject with an understood predicate.
rows.anchor: أولاها: أنه على إضمار فعل لما لم يمكن العطف، التقدير: وتلعنهم الملائكة

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliyah takes “all people” universally, including people cursing one another on the Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: فقيل ذلك يكون في القيامة، إذ يلعن بعضهم بعضا، ويلعنهم الله والملائكة والمؤمنون، فصار عاما، وبه قال أبو العالية.

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ, and Muqātil take “all people” to mean believers whose curses count.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد بالناس من يعتد بلعنته، وهم المؤمنون خاصة، وبه قال ابن مسعود، وقتادة، والربيع، ومقاتل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation includes unbelievers because, without realizing it, they curse themselves when saying “God curse the unbeliever.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: الكافرون يلعنون أنفسهم من حيث لا يشعرون، فيقولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The curse begins with God, then angels for their exalted rank and purity, and then people, whose condemnation by their peers is especially painful.
rows.anchor: ثم ثنى بالملائكة، لما في النفوس من عظم شأنهم وعلو منزلتهم وطهارتهم.

rows.speaker: أحمد
rows.claim: A report says Aḥmad answered his son’s question about cursing a named person by asking whether his son had ever seen him curse anything, then citing God’s curse on wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: وكما روي عن أحمد، أن ابنه سأله: هل يلعن؟ وذكر شخصا معينا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Abiding therein” most naturally refers to the curse, the nearest antecedent; another view supplies Hell, suggested by Quranic usage and the curse’s implication of Hell.
rows.anchor: خالدين فيها: أي في اللعنة، وهو الظاهر، إذ لم يتقدم ما يعود عليها في اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that punishment is not lightened may be a circumstantial clause within “abiding,” a second state from “upon them,” or an independent sentence.
rows.anchor: فهي حال متداخلة، أي حال من حال، لأن خالدين حال من الضمير في عليهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the earlier passage that denies their rescue, this passage denies that they will be granted any delay from punishment.
rows.anchor: وهنا: ولا هم ينظرون، نفى الإنظار، وهو تأخير العذاب.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that Quraysh asked Muhammad to describe and name their Lord, after which Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ and this verse were revealed.
rows.anchor: روي عن ابن عباس أنها نزلت في كفار قريش، قالوا: يا محمد، صف وانسب لنا ربك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Kaʿbah contained, or was surrounded by, 360 idols when this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: روي عنه أيضا أنه كان في الكعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address appears to include all creatures capable of worship; it may instead target Quraysh’s questioners or worshippers of idols, images, or fire.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الخطاب أنه لجميع المخلوقات المتصور منهم العبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “your God is one God,” wāḥid is formally an adjective but semantically the principal predicate; the strongest sense is that God has no peer, not that He is the first number.
rows.anchor: تقول: فلان واحد في عصره، أي لا نظير له ولا شبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed senses of the divine oneness are primordial uniqueness, having no parts, or being alone in deserving worship.
rows.anchor: والواحد المراد به نفي النظير، أو القديم الذي لم يكن معه في الأزل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “There is no deity but He” reinforces oneness by excluding every other deity and restricting divinity to God; the first clause affirms oneness and the second explicitly confines divinity.
rows.anchor: لا إله إلا هو: توكيد لمعنى الوحدانية ونفي الإلهية عن غيره.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān analyzes the exception pronoun as a substitute for the implicit pronoun in the omitted existential predicate, rather than a substitute for ilāh or for the nominative slot of lā.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر لي فيه أنه ليس بدلا من إله ولا من رجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nominative substitute is preferred for syntactic parallelism with its antecedent; accusative parsing as an exception is also permissible, with no disagreement known.
rows.anchor: غير أن الإتباع أولى للمشاكلة اللفظية، والنصب جائز، ولا نعلم في ذلك خلافا.

rows.speaker: المنتخب
rows.claim: Al-Muntakhab argues that “no deity but He” should not contain an ellipsis such as “for us” or “in existence”: either would narrow or merely repeat the absolute monotheism already stated.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز أن يكون في الكلام حذف، كما يقوله النحويون، والتقدير: لا إله لنا، أو في الوجود، إلا الله،

rows.speaker: المرسي
rows.claim: Al-Mursī calls that argument linguistically unsound: the nominal clause still needs an implicit predicate, and denying a deity’s essence entails denying its existence, contrary to the Muʿtazilī separation of essence and existence.
rows.anchor: هذا كلام من لا يعرف لسان العرب. فإن لا إله في موضع المبتدأ، على قول سيبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān agrees that a predicate is required but says generic existence is understood and may be omitted; a restricted predicate cannot be omitted without contextual evidence.
rows.anchor: وما قاله من تقدير خبر لا بد منه، لأن قوله: لا إله، كلام، فمن حيث هو كلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm show that the creator, nurturer, and promiser of a good afterlife deserves worship and obedience, while inspiring hope in His mercy.
rows.anchor: ذكر هاتين الصفتين منبها بهما على استحقاق العبادة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mercy verse follows a verse about the curse and punishment of those dying without monotheism, reflecting the Quranic alternation of punishment and mercy.
rows.anchor: وجاءت هذه الآية عقيب آية مختومة باللعنة والعذاب لمن مات غير موحد له تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān can be appositive to huwa, a new predicate introduced by an implied huwa, or a third predicate after “your God is one God” and “there is no deity but He.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز ارتفاع الرحمن على البدل من هو، وعلى إضمار مبتدأ محذوف، أي هو الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most grammarians reject describing a pronoun with al-Raḥmān, but al-Kisāʾī permits laudatory description of a third-person pronoun; Ibn Mālik omits the condition that the description be laudatory.
rows.anchor: وهو جائز على مذهب الكسائي، إذا كانت الصفة للمدح، وكان الضمير الغائب.

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says these two verses constitute God’s greatest name; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: روي عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: «إن هاتين الآيتين اسم الله الأعظم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After 2:163, Quraysh reportedly asked how one God could suffice all people, so this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: روي أنه لما نزل وإلهكم الآية، قالت كفار قريش: كيف يسع الناس إله واحد؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After asserting oneness and exclusive divinity, God presents wondrous creation as evidence from effect to agent and craft to maker, teaching people where to look and how to reason.
rows.anchor: استدل بهذا الخلق الغريب والبناء العجيب استدلالا بالأثر على المؤثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation may mean bringing the heavens and earth into existence, or composing and arranging their bodies and parts, as in describing someone’s fine form.
rows.anchor: وخلقها: إيجادها واختراعها، أو خلقها وتركيب أجرامها وائتلاف أجزائها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that khalq is redundant and the verse simply means “in the heavens and earth” is weak: Arabic does not establish redundant nouns, and creation arises from will rather than being will itself.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف، لأن زيادة الأسماء لم تثبت في اللسان، ولأن الخلق ليس هو الإرادة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavens are plural because they are distinct kinds, while earth is singular because all of it is soil; heaven is mentioned first for its rank, scale, and contents.
rows.anchor: وجمع السموات لأنها أجناس، كل سماء من جنس غير جنس الأحرى، ووحد الأرض لأنها كلها من تراب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among the heavens’ signs are their unsupported height, celestial bodies and their cycles, and their immense scale; astronomers give measurements for the sun, stars, and seven spheres.
rows.anchor: وآياتها: ارتفاعها من غير عمد تحتها، ولا علائق من فوقها، ثم ما فيها من النيرين

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān cites as sound the Prophet’s report that heaven groans, with no space of a foot lacking a prostrating angel.
rows.anchor: وقد صح عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: «أطت السماء وحق لها أن تئط، ليس فيها موضع قدم إلا وفيه ملك ساجد» . وصح أيضا:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth’s signs include its unsupported spread, waters, mountains, trees, terrain, minerals, and the different benefits and harms suited to each region.
rows.anchor: وآية الأرض: بسطها، لا دعامة من تحتها ولا علائق من فوقها، وأنهارها ومياهها وجبالها

rows.speaker: أرباب الهيئة
rows.claim: Astronomers describe earth as a point inside a circle, encircled by seas, air, fire, and the celestial spheres.
rows.anchor: وذكر أرباب الهيئة أن الأرض نقطة في وسط الدائرة ليس لها جهة

rows.speaker: الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Bāqillānī records disagreements among earlier thinkers about whether earth is stationary or moving, alongside varied speculative theories of the heavens.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكر القاضي أبو بكر محمد بن الطيب الباقلاني في كتابه المعروف (بالدقائق) خلافا عن الناس المتقدمين: هل الأرض واقفة أم متحركة؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Astronomical models rest on rational inference, not revelation; only God knows the created reality unless He discloses it by revelation.
rows.anchor: والذي تكلم عليه أهل الهيئة هو شيء استدلوا عليه بعقولهم، وليس في الشرع شيء من ذلك. والمعتمد عليه أن هذه الأشياء لا يعلم حقيقة خلقها إلا الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day may alternate by one succeeding the other, by light and darkness, or by length and shortness; Ibn Kaysān also says they may be equal.
rows.anchor: واختلاف الليل والنهار: اختلافهما بإقبال هذا وإدبار هذا، أو اختلافهما بالأوصاف في النور والظلمة، والطول والقصر، أو تساويهما، قاله ابن كيسان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view places night first because it was created first, citing the night stripped of day; another says light preceded darkness, affecting which night counts as the night of a given day.
rows.anchor: وقدم الليل على النهار لسبقه في الخلق، قال تعالى: وآية لهم الليل نسلخ منه النهار»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These competing definitions also affect legal interpretation of an oath not to speak during daytime.
rows.anchor: وكذلك ينبني على اختلافهم في النهار، اختلافهم في مسألة: لو حلف لا يكلم زيدا نهارا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah was the first to build a ship.
rows.anchor: والفلك التي تجري في البحر: أول من عمل الفلك نوح، على نبينا وعليه أفضل الصلاة والسلام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān continues a sound Prophetic report: the Inhabited House receives seventy thousand visitors each day, who never return before Resurrection.
rows.anchor: «أن البيت المعمور يدخله كل يوم سبعون ألفا، لا يعودون إليه إلى يوم القيامة»

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī says Gabriel told Noah to set the ship on a bird’s chest, making the ship an inverted bird with water below like air above.
rows.anchor: وقال له جبريل عليه السلام: ضعها على جؤجؤ الطائر. فالسفينة طائر مقلوب، والماء في أسفلها نظير الهواء في أعلاها، قاله أبو بكر بن العربي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ship’s sign is God’s subjection of it to float, stay above water despite its weight, and carry people to their destinations; a thrown stone would sink.
rows.anchor: وآيتها تسخير الله إياها حتى تجري على وجه الماء، ووقوفها فوقه مع ثقلها وتبليغها المقاصد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause highlights the ships’ continual renewed sailing; naming the sea reinforces their setting, and attributing motion to ships is figurative.
rows.anchor: ووصفها بهذه الصفة من الجريان، لأنها آيتها العظمى، وجعل الصفة موصولا، صلته تجري:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If mā is relative, ships travel carrying useful goods, with bāʾ indicating accompaniment; if it is a verbal noun, they benefit people’s trade and journeys, with bāʾ indicating cause.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن تكون ما موصولة، أي تجري مصحوبة بالأعيان التي تنفع الناس من أنواع المتاجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse mentions benefit rather than harm because the ships are presented as a divine favor.
rows.anchor: واقتصر على ذكر النفع، وإن كانت تجري بما يضر، لأنه ذكرها في معرض الامتنان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two min phrases in the rain clause may mark origin and then apposition, genus, or part; the second min phrase can attach to the verb despite the first min having a different sense.
rows.anchor: الأولى لابتداء الغاية تتعلق بأنزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fa links sending rain to the earth’s quick revival; revival and death are metaphors for visible plant growth and what remains dormant within the earth.
rows.anchor: وكنى بالإحياء عن ظهور ما أودع فيها من النبات، وبالموت عن استقرار ذلك فيها وعدم ظهوره.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Connecting “and He spread” to the preceding relative clauses requires a deleted return pronoun, but the grammatical conditions for deleting this prepositional pronoun are absent.
rows.anchor: إن قدرت هذه الجملة معطوفة على ما قبلها من الصلتين، احتاجت إلى ضمير يعود على الموصول، لأن الضمير في فيها عائد على الأرض

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī proposes connecting the phrase either to “sent down” or to “revived”; Abū Ḥayyān says both still require the missing pronoun.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: فإن قلت قوله: وبث فيها، عطف على أنزل أم أحيا؟ قلت: الظاهر أنه عطف على أنزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān supplies an omitted relative, reading “and what He spread in it of every creature,” as a separate sign of the remarkable forms, traits, movements, uses, and designs of land and sea creatures.
rows.anchor: والذي يتخرج على الآية، أنها على حذف موصول لفهم المعنى معطوف على ما من قوله: وما أنزل، التقدير: وما بث فيها من كل دابة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deleting a relative pronoun when context makes it understood is common in Arabic according to some grammarians, though Basrans do not accept it by analogy.
rows.anchor: وحذف الموصول الاسمي، غير أن عند من يذهب إلى اسميتها لفهم المعنى جائز شائع في كلام العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry supplies examples of omitting a relative pronoun: an unnamed poet omits the complement after “on whom,” and another line by Ḥassān omits “who praises him.”
rows.anchor: وإن لساني شهدة يشتفى بها ... وهو على من صبه الله علقم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also omits a relative in “and He sent down to you,” understood as “and what He sent down to you,” matching another verse’s “the Book sent down to His Messenger.”
rows.anchor: قولوا آمنا بالذي أنزل إلينا وأنزل إليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers distribute singular and plural forms among Quranic passages: Ḥamzah has singular exceptions at al-Furqān, al-Kisāʾī at al-Ḥijr, and other readers have their own exceptions.
rows.anchor: فأفرد حمزة إلا في الفرقان، والكسائي إلا في الحجر، وجمع نافع الجميع والعربيان إلا في إبراهيم والشورى، وابن كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥafṣ’s codex reads “spirits” here; the reciters agree on singular when the word has no definite article.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف حفصة هنا وتصريف الأرواح. ولم يختلفوا في توحيد ما ليس فيه ألف ولام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited recitations vary between singular and plural forms, with readers following different distributions across the passages.
rows.anchor: فأفرد حمزة إلا في الفرقان، والكسائي إلا في الحجر، وجمع نافع الجميع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran generally uses plural winds with mercy and singular wind with punishment, except the pleasant wind in Jonah; where the noun is indefinite, readers agree on the singular.
rows.anchor: وجاءت في القرآن مجموعة مع الرحمة مفردة مع العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān cites a supplication asking that winds be plural rather than singular; no transmitter or grading is given.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: «اللهم اجعلها رياحا ولا تجعلها ريحا» .

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says punishment wind is a single joined mass, while gentle mercy winds are dispersed; wind is singular for ships’ connected parts and disambiguated by “good.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: لأن ريح العذاب شديدة ملتئمة الأجزاء كأنها جسم واحد، وريح الرحمة لينة متقطعة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A singular reading may denote the generic and so convey the same sense as the plural.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بالتوحيد، فإنه يريد الجنس، فهو كقراءة الجمع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax permits “winds” to be nominative with taṣrīf annexed to its agent, or accusative with the source semantically annexed to its agent, meaning God directs the winds.
rows.anchor: والرياح في موضع رفع، فيكون تصريف مصدرا مضافا للفاعل، أي وتصريف الرياح، السحاب

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār calls clouds a sieve for rain, saying rain would ruin the earth without them; others say clouds draw rain from sky or earthly seas, or that God creates it within them.
rows.anchor: قال كعب الأحبار: السحاب غربال المطر، ولولا السحاب لأفسد المطر ما يقع عليه من الأرض.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Clouds are “subjugated” by holding heavy water aloft, delivering a measured amount where needed, withdrawing it afterward, or moving by winds; each account indicates divine oneness.
rows.anchor: وجعل مسخرا باعتبار إمساكه الماء، إذ الماء ثقيل، فبقاؤه في جو الهواء هو على خلاف ما طبع عليه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Between heaven and earth” is adverbial, governed either by “subjugated” or by an understood “being”; the emphatic lām enters because the predicate intervenes after inna.
rows.anchor: بين السماء والأرض: انتصاب بين على الظرف، والعامل فيه المسخر، أي سخر بين كذا وكذا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “for people” qualifies the signs; only rational people infer from these wonders God’s oneness, sole divinity, power, and wisdom.
rows.anchor: فإنه يشاهد من هذه الآية ما يستدل به على وحدانية الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed transmitted warning says woe to whoever recites the verse without digesting it, meaning without reflecting and taking heed.
rows.anchor: وقد أثر في الأثر: ويل لمن قرأ هذه الآية فمج بها، أي لم يتفكر فيها ولم يعتبر بها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse follows the oneness assertion by offering signs and blessings that prompt reflection, though they benefit only those able to reason with God-given intellect.
rows.anchor: ومناسبة هذه الآية لما قبلها، هو أنه لما ذكر تعالى أنه واحد، وأنه منفرد بالإلهية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There are eight signs, or nine if “He spread” begins a separate omitted-relative clause; they reduce to four categories: creation, alternation, rain, and direction.
rows.anchor: وهذه الأشياء التي ذكرها الله ثمانية، وإن جعلنا: وبث فيها، على حذف موصول،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation comes first as the greatest proof of divinity because it brings something forth from absolute nonexistence and implies God’s essential attributes.
rows.anchor: فبدأ أولا بالخلق، لأنه الآية العظمى والدلالة الكبرى على الإلهية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence moves from heavenly creation to effects of celestial bodies, then ships associated with earthly bodies, then shared rain and growth, and ends with winds and clouds that complete the preceding benefits.
rows.anchor: فانظر إلى هذا الترتيب الغريب في الذكر، حيث بدأ أولا باختراع السموات والأرض،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs fall into what intellect apprehends and what the eyes observe; reason traces visible signs back to the necessary existent, so the verse says “for people who reason,” not “who see.”
rows.anchor: فلذلك قال تعالى: لآيات لقوم يعقلون، ولم يقل: لآيات لقوم يبصرون،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After proving oneness, the verse contrasts those who take rivals with the clear evidence just presented; the general term people best includes both scriptural communities and idol worshippers.
rows.anchor: والأحسن حمله على الطائفتين من أهل الكتاب وعبدة الأوثان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For scriptural communities, rivals are leaders and rabbis whose commands followers obey even when they oppose God’s commands.
rows.anchor: فالأنداد، باعتبار أهل الكتاب هم رؤساؤهم وأحبارهم، اتبعوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For idol worshippers, rivals are statues treated as gods and worshipped alongside or instead of God.
rows.anchor: والأنداد، باعتبار عبادة الأوثان هي الأصنام، اتخذوها آلهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some restrict “people” to the People of the Book, others to idolaters; if restricted, Abū Ḥayyān favors the former, since the pronoun is rational and the following mutual disavowal better fits people than statues.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد بالناس الخصوص. فقيل: أهل الكتاب. وقيل: عباد الأوثان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min is either a relative subject or an indefinite noun qualified by the clause; yattakhidh is singular by agreement with the word man, and dun means other than in this construction.
rows.anchor: ومن: مبتدأ موصول، أو نكرة موصوفة، وأفرد يتخذ حملا على لفظ من،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says min dūn conveys that what follows lies outside the situation or sphere of the phrase’s subject, and translating it as “other than” does not always work.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ومن دون: لفظ يعطي غيبة ما يضاف إليه دون عن القضية التي فيها الكلام،

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh records dun as also meaning poor or inferior, as in calling a garment thūb dūn.
rows.anchor: وقد حكى سيبويه أيضا أنها تكون بمعنى رديء، تقول: هذا ثوب دون أي رديء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dun began as a spatial adverb for a lower place; “other than” develops by an implicit direction or place and omission of that noun, while anidād is the sole object of the derived verb.
rows.anchor: والذي ذكر النحويون، هو ما ذكرت لك من كونها تكون ظرف مكان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān continues the report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī: rivals are followed leaders whom people obey in disobedience to God.
rows.anchor: الرؤساء المتبعون، يطيعونهم في معاصي الله تعالى.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Qatādah identify the rivals as idols.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وقتادة: الأنداد: الأوثان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān prefers the general reading combining idols and leaders; the rational plural pronoun treats them collectively as objects of reverence and submission.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم لنا أن الأولى أن تكون الأنداد: المجموع من الأوثان والرؤساء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “they love them” may describe the rivals, state the unstated subject of yattakhidh, or qualify man; its plural verb follows man by meaning after yattakhidh followed it by form.
rows.anchor: والجملة من يحبونهم صفة للأنداد، أو حال من الضمير المستكن في يتخذ،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison “like God’s love” may be a circumstantial phrase or modify an omitted verbal noun; its implied active agent may be the addressees or the idolaters.
rows.anchor: الكاف في موضع نصب، إما على الحال من ضمير الحب المحذوف،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī interprets the phrase as equal glorification and submission to God; another reading compares their love of rivals with their love of God, since they acknowledged God and prayed sincerely at sea.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: كحب الله: كتعظيم الله والخضوع له، أي كما يحب الله،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says the verbal noun is formally attached to its object but implicitly has an omitted agent, variously understood as the addressees or the idolaters.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: حب: مصدر مضاف إلى المفعول في اللفظ،
